input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4: Brun cast Protection from Evil and Good on Corm and began the Naming. Check 7 (DC 12): she faltered around the forty-first name; the stone shuddered and the sleeper stirred, grieved and frightened, not yet hostile. The rite is stalled mid-recitation; it can be resumed with steadier words (a second try) if she speaks to the sleeper itself, not only the dead.

Corm's skin takes the glow of your spell, a thin silver shimmer along his scarred arm, and he draws a slow breath and nods. You open Father Dorrin's book, set your holy symbol to the cold iron, and begin.

The Morninglord's invocation comes steady and warm. The first names come easy, one after another, each laid down like a stone in a wall, and the dark behind the door seems to listen. Hild's lips move with every one. By the thirtieth the iron under your palm has gone from cold to faintly alive.

Then, near the forty-first, your tongue slips. The captain's script and the name you copied on the road blur together, and you hear yourself say a name wrong, a name that belongs to someone's mother. The words die in your mouth.

The door answers. A deep tremor rolls through the gallery, dust sifting from the timbers, and the heartstone flares and dims like a struck coal. From beyond the iron comes a sound that is not a roar, but a long, low, cracked note, grief as much as warning. Hild grabs the wall. Corm's arm shakes, but his hand stays flat on the stone, and your shimmer holds around him.

"It heard that," he says through his teeth. "It thinks we have named the wrong dead. It is afraid, Stonehearth, not angry yet. Say something true to it."

Your protection will hold for about four more minutes. The sixty-name rite is half done, and the sleeper is wide awake, listening.

What does Brun do?

sheet.name: Brunhilde Stonehearth

Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4: Religion 16 success. The Naming was spoken, sixty names with Brenn's last; the sleeper (a stone-spirit) was released with mercy. The door opened of itself; the lower galleries are still, the dead lie at rest. Hild and Corm will bring the sixty up for burial. Quest complete.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

The warding settles on Corm like a held breath, and you begin. The Morninglord's invocation first, then the names. Sixty of them, in the captain's order, each one set down in the quiet like a stone on a cairn. Hild's lips move with them. Garrick, at the bend, takes off his hood.

Around the thirtieth name the hum in your teeth changes. It is no longer a warning. It is a listening. By the fiftieth the iron under your holy symbol has gone warm as a hand, and Corm's shoulders are shaking, though his palm does not move. When you come to the last name, you say it plainly, the way you would call a child in from the rain: "Brenn Ironvein."

The heartstone lets go of the door with a sound like a long exhale. Cold, sweet air rolls out over your feet, and then it is only air. Something vast and old passes through the hill, slow as a tide going out, and you feel it as grief, then as relief, and then as nothing at all. The hand that held it has been loosened. The iron door swings inward on its own, and beyond it is only a dark gallery, still and clean.

Corm falls to his knees, weeping without sound. Hild kneels with him and holds him. In the dark beyond, at the edge of your lamplight, lie rows of shapes under old cloaks, laid out with care, and one of them has a hand resting on the stone floor as though it had been reaching out to hold something, and had been let go.

The sixty are at rest. The slope is quiet. You earn 200 XP, which brings you to 900, enough for level 3.

The sleeper is gone, the door is open, and the dead are waiting to be carried home. Your Protection spell is spent, and you have two first-level slots. Would you like to take your third level now, or first see to the dead with Hild and Corm?

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

Your hand is warm on Corm's shoulder, and the spell's quiet glow settles over him as you set your holy symbol to the iron. You speak the Morninglord's invocation, and then the names, one by one, each as if it were family's.

Somewhere past the twentieth name the iron under your symbol grows warm. By the fortieth, the heartstone is glowing the faint gold of a banked coal, and Corm's scarred arm is steady against it. You do not stumble, not once. The sixtieth is Brenn. You say it, and Hild makes a small sound behind you.

The door does not burst or crash. It swings inward on its own, slowly, with a long sigh like a held breath let go, and the sweetness in the air is gone. What comes up the dark stair is not a monster but light: a low, dim, patient light the color of wet slate, with the shape of a vast kneeling thing in it that is not quite shape. It is very old, and it is very tired.

It turns to you. You do not hear words. You feel them, in the hollow behind your breastbone: a small child, thin and cold, in a shaft that was falling, and a weight held up over her for three days and nights by something that did not know what it was holding, only that it was warm and alive. *You were not forgotten,* it says. *Thank you for the names.*

Then the light thins, rising, and in its going a figure walks out of it, a broad, grey-bearded dwarf in warden's leathers who stops before Hild and puts his palm to her cheek. You see Hild's face. You look away to give her that.

When the light is gone, the gallery is only a gallery, and the door stands open on a plain dark stair. Corm sinks to his knees, and then laughs, and then weeps, and Garrick, at the bend, quietly puts his bow on his shoulder and looks at the roof.

It is a little past six-twenty. The quest is done, and you have earned 200 XP: you are at 900, enough for level 3. Your Protection spell has ended with the rite.

Level 3 gives you a new spell level, 2nd-level slots, and a new domain spell. Shall we level up now, Brun?

Brun steps up to the door beside Corm, opens Father Dorrin's prayer book to the captain's rite, and sets her holy symbol against the cold iron. Before she begins, she casts Protection from Evil and Good on Corm, since his hand is the one on the stone, and says softly, "Steady, old friend. I'm here."

input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4: Brun spoke the Naming (Religion 15). The sleeper, a grieving stone-spirit, was released with mercy; the Iron-Banded Door unsealed, the foul air gone. Corm's keeper's burden ended. The remains of the sixty, Brenn among them, can now be carried up for burial; Brenn's was at rest with the spirit's hand held to the last.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

Your hand settles on the cold iron, over Corm's, and the warding light of Protection from Evil and Good rises around him like a held breath. You open Father Dorrin's book and begin.

The Morninglord's invocation comes first, plain and warm, and the hum in the door answers it, once, like a sleeper hearing a voice. Then the names. You say them slowly, one by one, as you said them in the dark, and with each, something in the gallery shifts: a sound like a long exhale, like stone settling after a hundred years of holding its breath. By the thirtieth, the iron bands beneath your palm are warm. By the fiftieth, Hild is weeping without a sound, her lips shaping each name beside you. Corm's arm trembles but does not move.

"Brenn Ironvein," you say last.

The heartstone brightens, a clear, soft gold like the first light on a snowfield. The door does not burst or crack. It opens as a hand opens, slowly, and beyond it lies not horror but a long, quiet gallery lit by the dawn that has somehow found its way down. No monster. Only a vast, slow breath, warm and sorrowful and then, at last, easing, like a child who has cried itself to sleep and wakes unafraid. Dust lifts and drifts upward in the light, and is gone.

Corm falls to his knees. The scar on his forearm has faded to a pale ghost. "It's finished," he whispers. "Forty winters... it's finished." Hild lays her hand on his shoulder, and then she walks into the gallery, calling her brother's name softly, and Garrick, lowering his bow, follows a respectful pace behind.

You have earned 200 XP: you are at 900 and may go up to level 3. The quest to mend the seal is done, and the long work of carrying Hearthdeep's dead home to their rest has begun.

Level 3 awaits. Shall we take it now? If so, I'll walk you through the choices.

line:
Brun falls into step beside Maren and shortens her stride to match. "Aunt Maren, while we walk, would you tell me about the Deepwatch itself, and about my mother as a girl? I'd like to hear the small things, like what she liked to eat and what songs she sang."

She glances ahead at Garrick and adds, "Garrick, thank you for the ford and the sheep trail. At the waymark-hut tonight I'll cook, since you've done the hard work all day."

input.add_to_description: Evening Day 5: at the waymark-hut on the saddle Brun found two sealed letters from Father Dorrin sewn into the prayer book's cover, addressed to the Deepwatch 'if she should ever come'. Maren says they never reached the Deepwatch. Seals unbroken. Maren shared small stories of Sigrun (hated barley porridge, loved honeyed oatcakes, sang a goat-and-lantern miners' round, drew maps on everything, counted 113 steps up to the Deepwatch door).

entries.text: time: 3 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 5:59 PM

Those two letters are the next thing on the table, and the calls that record them have just gone through. The clock now reads about six in the evening on Day 5.

The decision is yours, Brun. The seals are unbroken, and the letters are addressed to the Deepwatch, so you could open them here by the fire with Maren beside you, or carry them north sealed and give them to the Deepwatch's keepers yourself. What does Brun do?

Maren is quiet for a few strides, as if choosing which small thing to give first.

"The Deepwatch is a hall cut into the north face of a mountain, with a hundred and twelve steps up to its door, and every warden's child counts them aloud the first time. Your mother counted a hundred and thirteen, because she insisted the threshold was a step. She argued about it until she was grown."

You laugh, and it surprises you.

She tells you more as the road climbs. Sigrun hated barley porridge and would trade anything for honeyed oatcakes, so the cooks hid them from her in the lamp-oil store, and she found them anyway. She sang badly and loudly, a miners' round about a goat who swallowed a lantern, and the old surveyors pretended to be annoyed and hummed along in the tunnels. She drew maps in the margins of everything, her bread-board, her boots, once the back of her own hand. "She'd have drawn this road for you," Maren says, "and put a little goat on it."

Garrick, ahead, says nothing, but his pace eases. When you thank him for the ford he grunts, "Cook, then. I'll gather the wood," and that is all, which you take for a gladness.

Toward dusk you reach the saddle and the waymark-hut, a low round stone shelter with a turf roof and a hearth, the wardens' sign cut over the lintel. While Garrick cuts wood and Maren rests, you unwrap Father Dorrin's prayer book to hang it by the fire to air. Something slips from the cover's lining: two small, folded letters, sealed with plain wax and addressed in his cramped hand *To the Deepwatch, from Dorrin Ashbeard, if she should ever come*. They had been sewn into the binding all these years. The seals are unbroken.

Maren sees them and goes very still. "He wrote," she says. "He did write. Then they never reached us."

It is evening on Day 5, the stew is on, and you have three spell slots, Channel Divinity, and two letters in your hands. What does Brun do?

entries.text: time: 3 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 5:59 PM

Maren is quiet for a few strides, and then she talks, the way people do who have kept things a long time. She tells it to the road ahead rather than to you.

Sigrun, she says, hoarded honey-cakes like a dragon and was caught every time. She hummed a miner's counting song, *Seven Lamps Down*, whenever she worked, so that the whole hall knew where she was by the tune, and she measured everything with her thumb, even a loaf, even a cat. She chose surveying because she hated being told where a tunnel could not go. Maren hums three bars of the song, cracked and flat, and you realize, with a strange tug under the ribs, that you know the tune. You have hummed it all your life and never knew whose it was.

Of the Deepwatch she says it is built into the face of a high crag, its halls cut straight into the cliff, with a gatehouse on a stone bridge across a gorge. The wardens keep the Roll of Names there, a wall of slate plaques for every miner lost. "Fewer than forty of us now," she says. "We are a long memory with few hands." She glances at your pack. "Those two letters you carry, in Dorrin's hand, were meant for us. They were never sent. He will have had his reasons. We open them there."

By six the waymark-hut comes into sight on the saddle, a low stone shelter with a turf roof, a hearth, and a stack of dry peat. You cook as you promised: oatcakes toasted on the hearthstone, a pot of dried-apple porridge with a little salt pork Garrick produces from his pack. He eats two bowls without comment, which from him is a speech.

Outside, the sky goes violet over the hills. The saddle is quiet and the wind is steady. You are at full strength, three spell slots, Channel Divinity ready, with one more night on the road and the Deepwatch about a day and a half beyond.

Maren is quiet for twenty paces, and then she talks, in the slow, dry way of the very old.

The Deepwatch, she says, is not a fortress but a hall: a long gallery cut into the face of a cliff, with a great hearth at its heart that has not gone cold in six hundred winters. The wardens keep the ledgers there, and a wall of names, and a school for the children of the holds, where Sigrun learned her letters and her lines.

"She ate nothing but pickled onions and honey bread," Maren says, "and the cook swore she'd rot her teeth, and she never lost one. She sang badly. Loudly. The old miners' songs, the ones with the filthy verses, and she'd go red to the ears when she caught an elder listening." The corner of her mouth moves. "She sang you to sleep with one of them. I heard it once, when you were so small you fit in the crook of her arm."

You walk a while with that.

Then Maren says, more carefully, "Dorrin's book. Look in the cover lining, along the spine. He told me once, years ago, in a message that came too late, that he had written to us twice, and that he could not bring himself to send them."

You find them where she says, folded flat beneath the leather: two letters in his cramped hand, the wax seals unbroken, both addressed to the Deepwatch. You do not open them. Not yet. You tuck them back against the spine, and the book seems heavier and warmer in your hands.

The sun is low and gold by the time Garrick raises a hand ahead of you on the saddle. Below the crest a squat turf-roofed hut stands against the wind, with a warden's hammer-and-lines carved on its lintel and a hearth-stone swept clean. It is empty and dry, with wood stacked inside.

You said you would cook. It is half past five, and you have oatcakes, dried apple, two rations, and the innkeeper's wife's smoked cheese.

entries.text:
The sentry vanishes from the parapet, and for a long minute there is only the storm: rain hammering the bronze, wind howling along the cliff, and the lamps burning steady on either side of the doors. Maren's arm is thin and cold through your sleeve.

Then a bar the size of a roof-beam rises somewhere inside, and the great doors swing open on a warm gold hall.

Torvald Greycairn stands in the gap, flanked by two wardens with lanterns. He is a broad old dwarf with an iron-grey beard cut square, a captain's chain across his chest, and two fingers missing from his left hand. He looks at Maren first, and something in his jaw works. "Three days late, you stubborn old goat," he says, rough as gravel. "I had the bed aired twice."

"Torvald," she says, and that is all, and he takes her other arm so that she is held between the two of you.

Then he turns his eyes on you, and they are the same cold grey as a mountain tarn. He takes his time. He looks at your braid, your dented mail, your chin, and last at the ring on your finger.

"You have her chin," he says finally, grudging as a man pulling a tooth. "Gods rot it. You have the stubborn chin." He holds out his maimed hand. "The ledger, girl, if you would. And the ring, for a moment. I wrote the oath she broke, and I would see what is left of it."

Behind him the hall stretches away, hung with lamps, and somewhere far in there is a stair and a gallery and a wall of names.

Rain streams from your cloak. Garrick waits at your shoulder, bow unstrung, saying nothing. What does Brun do?

Your voice carries over the wind and the hiss of the rain, and the sentry goes very still above you. Then the lantern swings, a horn sounds twice inside the stone, and the great bronze doors begin to open with a groan of counterweights.

Warm light and the smell of lamp oil and hot bread spill out over you. Beyond the doors lies a long entry hall hung with lamps, and down its length comes a line of wardens with lanterns in their hands, silent, dwarves in grey cloaks pinned with the hammer-and-three-lines brooch, young and old, staring. At their head walks a stern, grey-bearded dwarf with one sleeve pinned empty at his shoulder and a voice you can hear before he uses it.

"Maren," he says, in a tone like a closing gate. "Three days late, and you bring the storm in with you." Then his eyes find you, and the iron goes out of his face all at once. He looks at your braid, at the chin, at the ring on your finger.

"By the hammer," says Torvald Greycairn softly. "Sigrun's child."

He lowers his lantern. He makes no speech. He simply puts his one hand on your shoulder, as you saw Hild do to Corm, heavy and warm and shaking a little. "You have your mother's walk," he says. "Come in out of the rain. All of you, the hunter too. There's stew, and a fire, and a great deal I owe you."

As you step over the threshold, the wardens close ranks behind you and the doors boom shut against the storm. In your pack, tucked into the binding of Father Dorrin's prayer book, you feel the stiff edge of two folded letters you had not noticed before, sewn there and sealed with his plain brown wax. They are addressed, in his small hand, to the Deepwatch.

It is nearly six. You are at 21 of 21, with three spell slots and Channel Divinity, warm and dry for the first time in a day. What does Brun do?

line:
Brun squares her shoulders, wipes the rain from her face, and calls up to the sentry in clear Dwarvish, "I'm Brunhilde Stonehearth, Sigrun's daughter, raised by Father Dorrin Ashbeard. I carry a copy of the Hearthdeep warden-captain's ledger, and I've come home."

She keeps one hand on Maren's arm and glances at Garrick. "Stay close, friend. You're with me, and you're welcome here."

input.add_to_description: Day 6 ~5:40 PM: Brun named herself at the gate. The bronze doors opened; Captain Torvald Greycairn came down to the gatehall himself. Dorrin's two hidden letters (in the binding of his prayer book) are recorded on Brun's sheet and are what Maren meant when she said Dorrin 'wrote to us'. Brun and Garrick are admitted as guests of the hall.

entries.text:
The sentry's lantern stops moving. For a long breath there is only the storm, the rain drumming on the bronze and the wind tearing at the lamps. Then the sentry says, in a changed voice, "Sigrun's daughter. Say it again." You say it again, and the lantern vanishes from the parapet at a run.

The great doors groan inward. Warm light and the smell of lamp-oil and baked bread pour out into the rain. Wardens crowd the gatehall in hooded cloaks, a few dozen of them, mostly grey-bearded, some barely past their apprenticeship, and they fall quiet as you step in. Someone takes Maren's other arm. Someone else, without a word, lifts your pack from your shoulders and sets a dry cloak about them. Garrick hangs back at the threshold with his bow lowered, and a young warden gestures him in with an awkward half-bow.

An old dwarf comes down the long stair at a measured pace. He is broad as a door, his beard iron-grey and braided in the wardens' fashion, a heavy chain of office across his chest, and a face carved of hard weather. This is Torvald Greycairn. He stops three paces from you and looks at your chin, then at the ring on your finger.

"She had that same jaw," he says. His voice is rough and low. "I told her it would get her killed." A pause. "I was wrong about the jaw. I was wrong about a good many things."

You remember what you are carrying. Beneath the cloth in your pack, in the binding of Father Dorrin's prayer book, lie the two letters he hid there, sealed in wax and addressed in his cramped hand to the Deepwatch. They are what he meant when he wrote to Maren. He never sent them. Your fingers find the spine of the book.

Torvald holds out a callused hand. "Come in out of the weather, Lantern of Hearthdeep. Yes, word has reached us. And Sigrun's daughter. There is a page in the Hall of Names that has waited a long time for you."

You are warm and dry for the first time in a day, your aunt is at your side, and Garrick is somewhere behind you being fed. You have 700 XP, 21 of 21 hit points, three spell slots, and Channel Divinity.

What does Brun do?

sheet.name: Brunhilde Stonehearth
sheet.opening: Brunhilde "Brun" Stonehearth, a stocky Hill Dwarf cleric of the Morninglord (Life domain), auburn braid threaded with brass beads, dented but polished chain mail, warhammer worn smooth at the grip, carries the prayer book of her late foster-father figure, Father Dorrin Ashbeard, the old priest who found her as a half-starved orphan in a collapsed mine shaft outside a hill-hold and raised her in his small shrine. She is optimistic, tries to find common ground even between fierce enemies, is suspicious of strangers, and wants to repay the mercy she was shown by walking into danger to keep others alive (ideal: Charity). Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. Keep the backstory true: Father Dorrin raised her long ago and she carries his book; nothing about it is recent or lost.
